text:
Every database query starts with a simple question: where is the data? Without an index, the answer is brutal. The database reads every row in the table, one after another, until it finds what you asked for. On a small table you'd never notice. On a big one, it's the reason your dashboard spins and your users leave.

An index works like the index at the back of a textbook. It's a separate, sorted structure, usually a B-tree, that maps the values you search on to where the matching rows actually live. Because a B-tree stays balanced and branches widely at every level, finding a value takes O(log n) steps instead of n. Even with millions of rows, the database only needs to visit a handful of nodes to reach the right one.

The payoff can be huge. In one case, a query against a 10-million-row table dropped from 2.1 seconds to 4 milliseconds once the right index was in place.

Indexes aren't free, though. Every insert, update, and delete now has to maintain the index too, which slowed writes by about 15%. Knowing when that trade-off is worth it is the real skill.
